lines.watchItem: Demand for leading-edge wafers still runs ahead of what the industry can build: TSMC's own tool demand sits at roughly 1.9 times the level projected nine months earlier, and it says it cannot meet chip demand while about 20 plants go up at once. Wafer-start plans across leading nodes are exposed to how long that gap stays open.

Advanced packaging is no longer the only thing rationing accelerator output: the leading vendor cut its next flagship to 192 gigabytes of stacked memory, and uncontracted stacked memory trades at four to five times the long-term contract price. Booked packaging slots can therefore still yield fewer finished systems than the allocation implies.

Custom accelerator silicon is scaling fast: Broadcom booked $16.7 billion of chip revenue for artificial-intelligence work in its third quarter, up 221% year over year, and points to $230 billion by fiscal 2028, while NVIDIA put $3.5 billion into MediaTek to bring a third designer onto its own connection fabric. The leading-node customer base tilts further toward custom designs alongside merchant accelerators.

The leading vendor now prices by power delivered rather than by chip, citing about $40 billion of revenue per gigawatt on its newest platform against $25 billion before and 35 times lower cost per token. End-market pricing stays firm, but memory suppliers hold the scarce input and capture a growing share of the value.

Public money is redrawing where supply gets built: South Korea announced a $919 billion plan for 8.4 gigawatts of data-center computing by 2029, with SK Group taking 2 gigawatts of Rubin systems and Naver a 200-megawatt order. A Chinese memory maker has meanwhile started small-batch stacked-memory production one generation behind the leaders, with local designers already testing it.

Contracted demand keeps building outside the cloud giants: one mid-size cloud says contracted revenue roughly doubled to about $103 billion, a robot maker signed an initial $3.5 billion commitment, and an enterprise hardware maker booked record orders of $3.1 billion for artificial-intelligence systems in a single quarter. Order books rather than shipments carry the demand signal this cycle.

Borrowed and third-party money funds a growing slice of accelerator purchases: a loan secured on chip-derived cash flows drew about $947 million of commitments against the far smaller sum sought, and a $45 billion compute agreement underpins one operator's expansion. That part of demand is exposed to credit conditions as much as to end-user appetite.

Land, power and building shells now set deployment timing alongside substrate, stacked memory and leading-edge wafers, and TSMC names construction labour and equipment delivery as its own limits into 2027. Site readiness decides when booked capacity turns into running systems.
